As of 115 AM EST Friday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: High pressure has begun to shift east and weaken off the 
east coast, now down to 1028mb per the latest RAP forecast. In doing 
so, a weak trough is beginning to work its way through the North 
Country, evident by slightly elevated water vapor and a thin band of 
mid to high clouds  draped from southwest to northeast. These clouds 
will work through the region into this morning, before clearing 
skies set in for this afternoon. A low level jet is also associated 
with the aforementioned shortwave, and in tandem with our steep 
inversion, will keep winds near summit levels elevated to 30 to 40 
MPH this morning, before abating towards this afternoon, with weaker 
flow aloft. Outside of the terrain, west winds today will help to 
increase our dewpoints and temperatures keeping our relative 
humidity values into the 40 to 50 percent range. Highs today will be 
quite similar to yesterday with value sin the mid 50s to near 60. 
Combined with the continued breezy conditions at summit levels, snow 
melt is highly likely, with the potential for any and all summit 
level snow to melt out. Thankfully summit level snow depths are only 
around a few inches, and therefore no impacts are expected for area 
waterways. Overnight lows tonight will dip into the low to mid 30s 
for southern and eastern Vermont, and in the low 40s for the St. 
Lawrence and the northern Champlain Valleys. 

Some terrain driven clouds across the eastern greens and Adirondacks 
will be possible Sunday as ridging begins to break down ahead of a 
coastal system Sunday. Temperatures will warm into the low 60s in 
the St. Lawrence with good southwest waa. Areas in Vermont will 
likely stay in the mid to upper 50s with less waa and better chances 
for some clouds. Widespread clouds will increase from the south to 
the north overnight Saturday.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Surface low pressure northeast of the Bahamas is 
beginning to take shape. The National Hurricane Center is monitoring 
the feature as well for potential tropical or subtropical 
development. Regardless of what the nature of this system is, there 
will be a tap of tropical moisture in the southeast flow ahead of 
the system as it tracks up the Mid-Atlantic Coast Sunday night. In 
some ways, the set up bears some resemblance to mesoband snowfall 
that moves laterally quasi-stationary. The highest deformation and 
frontogenesis will be positioned north of channeled southwesterly 
flow between anomalous heights in the Atlantic Ocean and an upper 
trough in northern Quebec of modest strength. A 120kt upper level 
jet will be positioned just to our north, aiding in synoptic lift. 
Lately guidance has trended the surface low moving north along the 
US East Coast further west, and some even tracking on shore. Some 
time should still be granted to determine if this is truly a trend, 
but there is some indication that from the eastern slopes of the 
Adirondacks and east into Vermont have some chance for moderate to 
heavy rainfall. Current reasonable worst case scenarios (90th 
percentile) have about 1-2" in this area. This rain will largely be 
beneficial, but as we enter the range of high resolution guidance, 
we may need to keep an eye out for any narrower region of higher 
rainfall totals considering the synoptic pattern. The coastal low 
will be racing north-northeast by Monday morning. Precipitation will 
quickly come to a close during the afternoon and evening, and there 
will likely be a non-diurnal temperature trend. Most max 
temperatures will occur mid-morning before steadily falling in brisk 
northwest winds.

KEY MESSAGE 3: Monday night into Tuesday, northwest winds will increase 
to 10-15 mph and gusts 25-30 mph as pressure gradients tighten as 
the surface low pressure exits while a strong surface high builds in 
its place. Today's NWP runs range around 1037-1041mb in terms of its 
strength, which is a little weaker than yesterday. Tuesday morning 
temperatures will likely settle into the 20s, and then struggle to 
lift above freezing during the day with brisk northwest winds 
continuing until the center of the strong high settles overhead 
Tuesday night into Wednesday. Trends have also sped up the surface 
high's eastward progression. This could allow for quicker moderation 
by Thanksgiving Day, but it may also pave the way for another 
coastal low to develop Thanksgiving and the day after. Given that 
it's roughly a week away, there is plenty of spread, but the recent 
cool air may allow for the onset of precipitation to be snow. 
However, warm south to southeast flow appears likely to make this a 
marginal temperature case with some potential for transitioning 
precipitation types. We'll continue to keep an eye, as this could 
impact post-holiday travel.
